identity_evidence.quote: A 48-year-old man (height 168 cm, weight 80 kg) with gastric cancer was scheduled for laparoscopic gastrectomy.

attribution_limitations: The text names surgical hours (third hour, fifth hour, eighth hour; glucose-insulin start from the fourth hour per the footnote) while Table 1 uses columns at 1, 3.5, 5.5, 6.5, 9.5 and 11 hours of surgery time. The text cites Table 1 for K+ 7.0 mEq/L in the third hour, but no column is labelled as the third hour (3.5 h shows 6.8, 5.5 h shows 7.0); K+ "exceeded 7" in the fifth hour while no column is labelled as the fifth hour. The source does not identify a text hour with a table column, so the text values are kept apart from the table cells as different time labels, not as two numbers for one value (no source conflict).

Postoperative potassium: the text gives 6.7 mEq/L after surgery, 7.0 mEq/L despite hemodialysis, and a peak on POD 1, while Table 1 has postoperative-hour columns (0, 3, 7, 12, 14, 20, 24, 48 h) with no POD labels; the highest table value is 8 at 3 h and the 24 h column shows 5.8. The source does not state that a text value and a table column are the same measurement, so these are different time labels, not a source conflict.
The abstract states a maximum serum K+ of 7.4 mEq/L during surgery; the source does not say which Table 1 cell it is, so it is kept as its own observation.

Certainty and cause of hepatic infarction: the CT is described as suggestive of infarction (text) or suggesting infarction (caption), while the abstract says CT revealed it and that retraction-related infarction would have exacerbated hyperkalemia, and the discussion states retraction caused infarction. The causal link to hyperkalemia is the authors' hypothesis.
The CT low-density area is placed in the left lobe of the liver in the text and in the lateral segment of the liver in the Fig. 2 caption; the observation keeps body site as liver.
The Table 1 footnote defines Hct and Glu, but the table has no Hct or Glu rows, so no such values are recorded. The lactate unit is printed as mg/dL and kept as printed.
The discussion lists possible contributors to preoperative or early hyperkalemia (renal failure, insufficient hemodialysis, potassium-containing food or drink) as possibilities only.
Fig. 1 plots AST and ALT over time without printed values; the caption expands ALT as alkaline aminotransferase while the text uses alanine aminotransferase.
